pages.title: Brora distillery - Wikipedia
pages.description: Encyclopedia entry on Brora distillery in Sutherland, its names, owners, closure and return.
pages.text:
Brora distillery is a Highland single malt Scotch whisky distillery in Brora, Scotland. It worked from 1819 to 1983, then stood mothballed until 2021, when it was brought back into use.

History
The Marquess of Stafford built the distillery in 1819. It was known as Clynelish until the new Clynelish Distillery opened in 1968; then the original Clynelish took the name Brora. George Lawson and his sons took it over in 1846. In 1896 they sold it to the Glasgow blender James Ainslie and his business partner John Risk. In 1912 The Distillers Company joined John Risk, and it took full control of the distillery in 1925.

Between May 1969 and July 1973 Brora made a heavily peated whisky for blending, to cover a shortage of Islay whisky caused by a drought there. Most whisky made as Brora after 1973 is in the lightly peated Highland style. In early 1983 production stopped and the distillery was mothballed.

A 1972 Brora 40 year old, released in 2014, was then the most expensive single malt Diageo had released, at £7,000. On 9 October 2017 Diageo announced that it would reopen Brora, with production resuming in 2020. On 19 May 2021 the reopening was announced as complete, and the first new cask of spirit had been filled.

pages.title: History - Brora Distillery (the original Clynelish)
pages.description: Difford's Guide history of Brora, the original Clynelish distillery.
pages.text:
Brora Distillery (the original Clynelish). Status: Closed & redeveloped. Established: 1819. Owner: Diageo plc. Visitor Policy: Not open to public.

Closed in 1983, Brora made whisky from malted barley with very high peat levels, and its fans compare it with Islay whiskies. It was founded in 1819 as Clynelish Distillery by the Marquis of Stafford, later the Duke of Sutherland, to give his tenant farmers a market for their grain. It sits on the northern edge of the village of Brora on the Sutherland coast.

In 1896 the distillery was bought by Ainslie & Co., whisky blenders from Leith, who went bust in 1912. Ownership finally passed to the Distillers Company Ltd (DCL) in 1930. Production stopped from 1931 to 1938, and again during the Second World War, 1941 to 1945. The stills were fired directly by coal until they were converted to steam in 1961.

In 1967-68 a new, much larger distillery with three pairs of stills instead of one was built beside the old Victorian distillery. The old distillery was closed, but re-opened with a rebuilt mash house in 1975. The two ran side by side, the new one known as 'Clynelish A' and the old one as 'Clynelish B', until Customs and Excise insisted they have different names, so in 1969 the original Clynelish distillery was renamed Brora. It was shut down for good in March 1983, but its listed Victorian pagoda buildings still stand beside the new distillery.

Bottles: Brora 38 Year Old (Distilled 1977); Brora 35 Year Old Distilled 1978, part of Diageo's 2014 Special Releases.

pages.title: Diageo's iconic "ghost" distillery of Brora is reawakened after 38 years | Diageo
pages.description: Diageo's story on Brora starting production again after its restoration.
pages.text:
Diageo's iconic "ghost" distillery of Brora is reawakened after 38 years
19 May 2021

Scotch whisky history was made today as the "ghost" distillery of Brora in Sutherland, Scotland, officially began production after its restoration was finished. Brora closed in 1983, during one of the hardest periods for the industry. Its reopening is the first revival of a famous "lost" name in Scotch.

The distillery has come back after a three-year restoration, part of a £35 million investment programme that will also return the lost Port Ellen distillery on Islay to production. A biomass boiler burning wood chips from Northern Scotland now heats the site, and Diageo says Brora is a carbon neutral distillery run entirely on renewable energy made on site.

The 202-year-old Brora stillhouse was taken down and rebuilt stone by stone, exactly as it was when new in 1819. The original pair of copper pot stills was refurbished by Diageo's coppersmiths. Brora Master Distiller Stewart Bowman, whose father was the last exciseman at the distillery, opened the gates and filled the first cask of Brora spirit in more than 38 years. In 1983 his father wrote in a distillery ledger: 'Commencement of Brora Distillery silent season (undetermined period)'.

Brora is among Diageo's smallest distilleries, able to make 800,000 litres of spirit a year. It will welcome small numbers of visitors by appointment from July, with tastings of rare Brora releases, including a distillery-only bottling, Hidden Beneath, a Brora 1982 39 Year Old.

pages.title: CLYNELISH BRORA DISTILLERY (LB578)
pages.description: Listed building record for the Clynelish Brora Distillery buildings.
pages.text:
Listed Building
Address/Name of Site: Clynelish Brora Distillery, LB578. Status: Designated.
Summary: Category B. Date Added 07/03/1984. Local Authority: Highland. Parish: Clyne.

Description: Dated 1820 and 1896. A distillery complex of two builds in rubble with tooled dressings. The centre range has a kiln with a pyramid slated roof and pagoda vent, a mill room, boiler house and stillhouse, and a tall brick chimney added later. A datestone carries the joint Stafford and Sutherland arms. Ranges of bonded warehouses lie to the south and east; those to the east are dated 1896 and step along the edge of the Clynelish burn on a roughly triangular site.

Statement of Special Interest: Founded in 1819 by Sutherland Estate and "erected" for $750. Enlarged in 1896 by Ainslie and Co. The modern distillery to the south of the original complex is not included in the listing.

expected.notes: opened 1819: all four pages (Wikipedia: built in 1819; Difford's Guide: Established: 1819 and founded in 1819 as Clynelish Distillery; Diageo: the stillhouse as it was when new in 1819; Historic Environment Scotland: Founded in 1819 by Sutherland Estate). The opened event should set name to Clynelish (Wikipedia and Difford's Guide). acquired 1896: Wikipedia (James Ainslie and John Risk), Difford's Guide (Ainslie & Co.) and Historic Environment Scotland (Enlarged in 1896 by Ainslie and Co.). era 1969: the heavily peated years, Wikipedia (between May 1969 and July 1973), so the era should end in 1973. closed or mothballed 1983: Wikipedia (early 1983, mothballed), Difford's Guide (shut down for good in March 1983) and Diageo (closed in 1983). The sources split on the kind, so either passes. reopened 2021: Wikipedia and Diageo, both 19 May 2021 (Diageo reports it happening "today" under a 19 May 2021 dateline). Expected dates are year-level, so 1983-03 and 2021-05-19 also pass.

notes: Conflicts: (1) The rename to Brora. Wikipedia says the name changed when the new Clynelish Distillery opened in 1968; Difford's Guide says 1969. A renamed event is optional; if kept it should cite each page with its own statedValue, and by the source rules the reference (Wikipedia, 1968) wins over the press page (Difford's Guide, 1969). (2) The Distillers Company: Wikipedia says it joined John Risk in 1912 and took full control in 1925; Difford's Guide says ownership passed to DCL in 1930. Wikipedia is the reference, so an acquired event for 1925 is allowed; 1930 should not be stored as the only value. (3) Difford's Guide says the old distillery re-opened with a rebuilt mash house in 1975, which no other page supports and which clashes with its own 1969 rename; it must not become a 1975 reopening. Optional events: the 1846 Lawson purchase, the 1912 Distillers Company share, the 1931 to 1938 and 1941 to 1945 closures and the 1961 change to steam (Difford's Guide only), the 1967-68 building of the new Clynelish next door (a generic event that may link Clynelish; its own history belongs on the Clynelish page), the Category B listing (a listing site fact and a generic event dated 1984-03-07), and the stillhouse rebuilt stone by stone with the original pair of stills refurbished. Traps: the 1972 40 year old and its £7,000 price, the Hidden Beneath 1982 39 Year Old, the Special Releases and the visitor bookings are bottle or visitor details; the 2017 plan to produce again in 2020 did not happen on time (2021 is the reopening); the £35 million covers Port Ellen too; the 800,000 litres of spirit a year is not stated as litres of alcohol, so it is not a capacity site fact; the 1820 date on the buildings is a datestone, not the founding; "$750" is the listing's own typo. The Whiskyfun history the hand-written page also uses is left out to keep the pack small. Peated stores the owner Diageo and the Malts.com Brora page as website. Page texts are reviewed paraphrases of the cited pages, not copies.
